content: Threatened miscarriage is a condition that affects approximately 10% to 15% of all pregnancies. It is characterized by vaginal spotting or bleeding during early pregnancy, and nearly half of these cases result in pregnancy loss. Currently, there is no effective preventive treatment available for this condition. Chinese herbal medicines have been used for centuries in Asian countries and have recently gained popularity as an alternative to Western medicine. Many studies suggest that these herbal remedies may help prevent miscarriage, but there has been no comprehensive evaluation of their effectiveness in cases of threatened miscarriage. The objective of this review was to assess the therapeutic effects of Chinese herbal medicines in the treatment of threatened miscarriage. To achieve this, a thorough search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register, Chinese Biomedical Database, China Journal Net, China National Knowledge Infrastructure, WanFang Database, Chinese Clinical Trial Registry, EMBASE, CINAHL, PubMed, Wiley InterScience, and the International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. The search covered studies published up to January 31, 2012. Additionally, reference lists of retrieved studies were reviewed, and experts in the field, as well as herbal medicine manufacturers, were contacted for further information. The review included randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared Chinese herbal medicines (used alone or in combination with other treatments) to placebo, no treatment (including bed rest), or other pharmaceuticals for the treatment of threatened miscarriage. Two independent reviewers assessed the studies for inclusion, evaluated the risk of bias, and extracted data, which were then verified for accuracy. A total of 44 randomized clinical trials involving 5100 participants were included in the review. However, none of the trials used placebo or no treatment (including bed rest) as a control. The analysis revealed that the effectiveness of Chinese herbal medicines alone, in terms of continuing pregnancy beyond 28 weeks of gestation, was not significantly different from that of Western medicines alone (average risk ratio [RR] 1.23; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.96 to 1.57; based on one trial with 60 women). On the other hand, the combination of Chinese herbal medicines with Western medicines was found to be more effective than Western medicines alone in continuing pregnancy beyond 28 weeks (average RR 1.28; 95% CI 1.18 to 1.38; based on five trials with 550 women). The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to determine the effectiveness of Chinese herbal medicines alone for the treatment of threatened miscarriage. However, the combination of Chinese herbal medicines with Western medicines appears to be more effective than Western medicines alone. It is important to note that the quality of the included studies was poor, and further high-quality research is needed to better evaluate the effectiveness of Chinese herbal medicines in this context.
